title: Sub-Rayleigh Imaging of Unequal-Intensity Sources: Near-Quantum-Limit Multiparameter Estimation
authors: Y. Batuhan Yilmaz, Kent A. G. Bonsma-Fisher, Muhammad Mohid, Noah Lupu-Gladstein, Arthur O. T. Pang, Aephraim M. Steinberg
abstract: In optical imaging, diffraction strongly degrades the performance of conventional intensity-based estimation once the separation between two sources is below the Rayleigh-Abbe limit. Recent developments showed that this limitation can be surpassed using spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE), and this was demonstrated in several experiments for two equal-intensity spots of unknown separation. When there are multiple unknown parameters, as in the case of several unequal sources with unknown intensities and unknown separation, cross-talk among the parameters makes the multi-parameter estimation problem significantly more challenging. In this paper, we adapt super-resolved position localization by inversion of coherence along an edge (SPLICE) to estimate both the separation and relative intensity of two incoherent sources simultaneously. We demonstrate a clear advantage over direct imaging (DI), achieving a root mean squared error (RMSE) approximately $50 \%$ larger than the quantum limit and a sixfold improvement over DI within the range of parameters we tested. This improvement can be even greater for smaller separations and larger intensity imbalances when crosstalk is suppressed.
summary: This paper presents a method called SPLICE to overcome diffraction limitations when measuring two closely spaced light sources with unequal intensities. By adapting super-resolution localization techniques and using quantum information theory bounds, the authors demonstrate that their approach significantly improves the accuracy of estimating both separation and intensity compared to standard direct imaging methods. This work advances the field by achieving near-quantum-limit precision in complex multiparameter optical estimation.
main_problem: The core problem is overcoming the diffraction limit (Rayleigh criterion) in optical imaging to simultaneously estimate both the separation ($\delta$) and relative intensity ($q$) of two spatially unresolved, unequal-intensity light sources.
main_result: The proposed SPLICE method significantly outperforms Direct Imaging (DI), achieving an estimation precision that approaches the quantum limit with up to a sixfold improvement over DI in tested regimes.
method: The authors adapt Super-Resolved Position Localization by Inversion of Coherence along an Edge (SPLICE) technique, employing quantum parameter estimation theory based on Fisher Information matrices derived from measured photon counts.
model_or_system: The system involves two incoherent light sources whose combined field is imaged. The analysis models the state as a statistical mixture and uses projectors onto specific spatial modes (Hermite-Gauss functions) to extract information about $\delta$ and $q$.
key_observables: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for estimated separation ($\hat{\delta}$) and relative intensity ($\hat{q}$); Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound (QCRB).
important_parameters: Separation ($\delta$), relative intensity ($q$), beam radius ($\sigma$), quantum limit bounds, and cross-talk parameter ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes single-photon detection dominates, the center of mass is known, and theoretical bounds rely on asymptotic unbiasedness (large photon number).
figures_summary: Figures compare estimated vs. true values for $\delta$ and $q$, showing SPLICE's superior performance relative to DI; one figure plots the ratio of CRBs demonstrating SPLICE's growing advantage as separation decreases.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the limitations of classical imaging, introduces the theoretical framework using quantum Fisher Information matrices (CRB), details the adaptation of SPLICE for multiparameter estimation, and concludes with experimental validation showing performance approaching the quantum limit.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems as it pushes measurement techniques beyond classical limits by exploiting quantum correlations in parameter estimation, which has implications for sensing and imaging.
